checked_sources: Kan et al. 2017 full text (public PDF, sunwaymedical.com)
Barry et al. 2007 abstract (Europe PMC, PMID 17911042)
Park et al. 2026 full text (Europe PMC PMC13457458, Tables 1 and 2)
Schumacher et al. 2020 full text (Europe PMC PMC7178985, Tables 1 and 2, Methods)
evidence_location: Kan 2017: Methods p. 433-434 (n = 50 university students, mean age 22.7, PHQ-9/DASS-21 screened; two 2-min sessions eyes closed and open; 16 observed sites Fp1...O2 although 32 loci were recorded) and Results p. 436 (global mean theta 12.41 kuV^2 eyes closed vs 14.21 eyes open; global mean alpha 20.0 vs 5.08 kuV^2; alpha significantly higher within all brain regions eyes closed). Barry 2007: abstract Methods/Results (28 university students; across-scalp mean absolute delta, theta, alpha and beta reduced from eyes closed to eyes open; decreased posterior/increased frontal beta eyes open). Park 2026: abstract and Table 1 (608 participants aged 20-70, 3,229 recordings), Table 2 (occipital alpha relative power, EO vs EC beta = -0.2197, SE 0.0038, 95% CI -0.2271 to -0.2124). Schumacher 2020: Table 1 (HC N = 40, age 73.4 +/- 6.6), Table 2 (HC eyes-closed alpha power 49.1 [41.9, 56.3], eyes-open 18.9 [16.1, 21.7]), Methods (relative power around the individual alpha peak +/- 2 Hz at O1, Oz, O2).
quote: The global mean of the alpha-range power during eyes-closed state was 20.0 kµV2 vs. 5.08 kµV2 for eyes-open
discrepancy: No number or attribution is off. Two nuances the statement drops: (1) in Kan 2017 'theta slightly higher with the eyes open' holds only for the global mean (14.21 vs 12.41 kuV^2); regionally theta was significantly higher eyes open at Fp1/Fp2 but significantly higher eyes closed at C3, C4, P3, P4, O1, O2, T3 and T5. (2) Kan's abstract says 'all brain regions (32 EEG channels)' while the analysis reports 16 sites; the claim's 16 is the analyzed set. The last sentence (alpha x4, beta x0.8 eyes closed, mu unchanged) is the site's model choice; no source gives a 0.8 beta factor, and Barry's across-scalp beta is lower eyes open, so x0.8 eyes closed matches the sources only for a frontal beta region (Barry: increased frontal beta eyes open; Kan: prefrontal beta higher eyes open). 49.1/18.9 = 2.6 and 20.0/5.08 = 3.9, as stated.
suggested_fix: Set status verified. Optional precision: 'the global mean theta was slightly higher with the eyes open (14.21 vs 12.41 kuV^2), driven by the prefrontal sites; at central, parietal, occipital and temporal sites theta was higher with the eyes closed'. If the beta x0.8 factor is kept, say it represents a frontal beta region (Barry 2007 found across-scalp beta lower, but frontal beta higher, with the eyes open).
bibliographic_issues: None. Kan 2017: Neurophysiology Vol. 49, No. 6, December 2017, pp. 432-440, DOI 10.1007/s11062-018-9706-6 as printed on the PDF (received 2015, DOI issued 2018). Barry 2007: Clin Neurophysiol 118(12):2765-2773 confirmed. Park 2026: Front Aging Neurosci 18:1869339, PMID 42582254, PMCID PMC13457458 confirmed. Schumacher 2020: Alzheimers Res Ther 12(1):46 confirmed.

checked_sources: Chikhi et al. 2022 abstract (Europe PMC, PMID 35128686)
Scharinger et al. 2017 full text (Europe PMC PMC5263141, Methods 'Data Preprocessing and Analysis' and Results 'Theta ERS'/'Alpha ERD')
Gevins et al. 1997 abstract (Europe PMC, PMID 9177767)
Brouwer et al. 2012 abstract (Europe PMC, PMID 22832068; IOP full-text page could not be opened)
evidence_location: Chikhi 2022 abstract: '45 effect sizes from 24 studies involving 723 participants'; theta g = 0.68, CI [0.41, 0.95]; alpha g = -0.25, CI [-0.45, 0.04]; beta g = 0.50, CI [0.21, 0.79] (all match). Scharinger 2017: Participants (20 university students, mean age 25.15); Methods: ERD/ERS% computed 'with respect to a baseline. As baseline we used the mean frequency band power of the low-load category (i.e., the averaged power over the entire epoch length of the low-load condition) for each task individually'; theta analyzed in the frontal-central ROI, alpha in the parietal-occipital ROI, in an early (0-1000 ms) and a late (1000-2000 ms) post-stimulus window. Results: theta ERS, late window, N-back low 8.75% vs medium 18.48% (p = 0.009), high 16.78% (n.s.); alpha ERD, early window, N-back low -5.63% vs medium -24.44% (p < 0.001), high -20.29% (n.s., 'we did not observe any further increase'). Gevins 1997 abstract: 8 subjects, 115 channels; frontal midline theta increased with memory load; slow parietocentral alpha decreased. Brouwer 2012 abstract: 'All our ERP, power and fusion models provide classification accuracies between 80% and 90% ... after 2 min'; 'For 32 out of 35 participants, classification was significantly higher than chance level after 2.5 s (or one letter) as estimated by the fusion model'.
quote: As baseline we used the mean frequency band power of the low-load category
discrepancy: (1) Scharinger 2017: the percentages are not 'relative to a pre-stimulus reference'; they are ERD/ERS% relative to the mean band power of the low-load condition over the whole epoch (per task). The only pre-stimulus baseline in the paper (-150 ms) is for the ERPs. Also the theta values come from the late window (1000-2000 ms) and the alpha values from the early window (0-1000 ms), which the claim does not say; the numbers themselves (8.75, 18.48, -5.63, -24.44) and 'no further change at high load' are correct. (2) Brouwer 2012: the '32 of 35 participants above chance after 2.5 s' result is for the fusion model (ERP + spectral power features), not for spectral power features alone; the 80-90% after 2 min holds for all three model types including power. All Chikhi and Gevins numbers match.
suggested_fix: Set status partially (or verified after rewording): '... in 20 adults doing an n-back task, frontal theta synchronization measured against the mean power of the lowest load rose from 8.75% at low to 18.48% at medium load (1 to 2 s after each stimulus) and parietal alpha desynchronization from -5.63% to -24.44% (first second after each stimulus), with no further change at high load; ... spectral power features told the highest from the lowest n-back level at 80 to 90% after 2 min of data, and a model combining spectral power with event-related potentials was above chance after 2.5 s for 32 of 35 participants.'
bibliographic_issues: None. Chikhi: Psychophysiology 59(6):e14009 confirmed. Scharinger: Front Hum Neurosci 11:6 confirmed. Gevins: Cereb Cortex 7(4):374-385 confirmed. Brouwer: J Neural Eng 9(4):045008 confirmed; author initials in Europe PMC are 'van Erp JB' (site: JBF), a harmless variant.

checked_sources: Pope et al. 1995 abstract (Europe PMC, PMID 7647180)
Marcantoni et al. 2023 full text (Europe PMC PMC10346153, abstract and Discussion)
Arns et al. 2013 abstract (Europe PMC, PMID 23086616)
Magosso et al. 2019 full text (Europe PMC PMC6614966, Participants 2.1 and Results 3.1)
evidence_location: Pope 1995 abstract: subjects 'run in the closed-loop feedback configuration under four candidate and three experimental control definitions of an engagement index'; 'an index constructed according to the formula, beta power/(alpha power + theta power), reflected task engagement best'. Marcantoni 2023: abstract ('82 documents resulted'; '37 different formulations of involvement indexes'); Discussion: 'the most frequently used are I1 (β/α), I2 (β/(α + θ)), I3 (β/θ), and I4 (θ/α), including their derived forms'. Arns 2013 abstract: 'Nine studies ... 1253 children/adolescents with and 517 without ADHD'; ES 0.75 (6-13 years) and 0.62 (6-18 years); 'decreasing difference in TBR across years, explained by an increasing TBR for the non-ADHD groups'; 'Excessive TBR cannot be considered a reliable diagnostic measure of ADHD'. Magosso 2019: section 2.1 'Thirty healthy volunteers ... took part in Experiment 1. Forty-one healthy volunteers ... took part in Experiment 2. Participants in the two experiments were different'; Results 3.1: alpha power 'larger decrease (by about 0.15 points) during the arithmetic task than that during the reading numbers task across all electrodes' (normalized to the pre-task eyes-open relaxation phase r1 = 1); 2 x 2 ANOVA main effect of Region F(1,29) = 23.9 ('alpha power decreased more posteriorly than anteriorly') and of Task Type F(1,29) = 24.1.
quote: Thirty healthy volunteers ... took part in Experiment 1. Forty-one healthy volunteers ... took part in Experiment 2
discrepancy: Magosso 2019: the mental arithmetic versus number reading comparison (Experiment 1, the source of the 'about 0.15' and the parieto-occipital versus fronto-central effect) had 30 participants, not 41; the 41 participants were a different group in Experiment 2 (virtual-reality immersion), which does not include the number-reading task. The auditor note's reading '41, with 30 in the ANOVA' is a conflation of the two experiments. Arns 2013: the claim omits that the abstract calls the 0.75 and 0.62 effect sizes 'misleading and considered an overestimation' because heterogeneity remained significant, and that TBR was judged to have prognostic value in a sub-group. Pope 1995 and Marcantoni 2023 fully supported (the 'four most used' is stated in the Discussion as 'most frequently used', including derived and reciprocal forms).
suggested_fix: Set status partially until corrected, then verified: replace '(41 participants)' with '(30 participants)'. Optional: 'effect sizes of 0.75 at ages 6 to 13 and 0.62 at 6 to 18, which the authors called overestimates because the studies were heterogeneous, and which shrank over the years ...'.
bibliographic_issues: None. Pope: Biol Psychol 40(1-2):187-195 confirmed. Marcantoni: Sensors 23(13):5968, PMCID PMC10346153 confirmed. Arns: J Atten Disord 17(5):374-383 confirmed. Magosso: Comput Intell Neurosci 2019:7051079, PMCID PMC6614966 confirmed.

checked_sources: Tran et al. 2020 abstract (Europe PMC, PMID 32108954)
Lal & Craig 2002 Psychophysiology abstract (Europe PMC, PMID 12212650)
Lal & Craig 2002 RS2002 conference paper, full PDF read through WebFetch (archive.acrs.org.au/files/arsrpe/RS020004.PDF; direct curl fails on the host's certificate name mismatch)
Jap et al. 2009 abstract via the UTS OPUS repository record (opus.cloud1.lib.uts.edu.au/handle/10453/8938; ScienceDirect page not retrievable)
De Gennaro et al. 2001 abstract (Europe PMC, PMID 11595150)
evidence_location: Tran 2020 abstract: 21 studies; overall increase g = 0.68 (95% CI 0.24-1.13), 'medium effect size (using Cohen's g)'; theta g = 1.03 (0.79-1.60), alpha g = 0.85 (0.47-1.43), 'small to moderate changes found in delta and beta bands'; 'Central regions of the scalp showed largest change (g = 0.80)'; 'large increases in theta activity in frontal, central and posterior sites (all g > 1)'. Lal & Craig 2002 Psychophysiology abstract: 'driver simulator task in 35 randomly selected subjects'; 'Delta and theta activity were found to increase significantly during fatigue'. Conference paper: Methods 'A total of forty male subjects, 20 professional truck drivers' (plus 20 non-professional), simulator task, 'average EEG magnitude (µV) was computed as an average of the nineteen channels'; Table 1 (changes from alert baseline, mean +/- SD, in µV): delta up to 21.1 (non-professional, post-transitional), theta up to 3.1 (non-professional, post-transitional; 3.0 at transition), alpha up to 1.4 (non-professional), beta up to 1.2 (professional); pages 502-507. Jap 2009 abstract: 52 subjects (36 males, 16 females), monotonous driving session; four algorithms (θ+α)/β, α/β, (θ+α)/(α+β), θ/β all increased over time, (θ+α)/β most; 'stable delta and theta activities', 'a slight decrease of alpha activity', 'a significant decrease of beta activity (p < 0.05)'. De Gennaro 2001 abstract (7 subjects): conclusion '(a) the alpha rhythm spreads anteriorly as the transition progresses'.
quote: large increases in theta (g = 1.03; 95%CI: 0.79-1.60) and alpha bands (g = 0.85; 95%CI: 0.47-1.43)
discrepancy: All numbers and attributions check out. Minor points: (1) the conference-paper maxima are 21.1 and 3.1 µV (the claim rounds to 21 and 3 while keeping 1.4 and 1.2 to one decimal), and they are group means of 20-driver subgroups in different fatigue phases (beta's 1.2 is the professional group, the other three the non-professional group), not individual values; (2) Jap 2009's abstract does not itself say the ratios rose 'mainly through a fall in beta'; it reports delta and theta stable, alpha slightly decreased and beta significantly decreased, from which that reading follows; (3) Tran 2020 labels its statistic 'Cohen's g'; the claim writes 'g' without a name, which is fine; (4) De Gennaro's conclusion is phrased 'as the transition progresses' (7 subjects), the claim's 'before sleep onset' is consistent with the abstract's pre-onset occipital prevalence of >8 Hz activity.
suggested_fix: Set status verified. Optional precision: 'by up to 21.1 µV (delta), 3.1 µV (theta), 1.4 µV (alpha) and 1.2 µV (beta), as group means' and 'rose, with beta the only band that fell significantly'.
bibliographic_issues: None. Tran: Psychophysiology 57(5):e13554 confirmed. Lal & Craig: Psychophysiology 39(3):313-321, DOI 10.1017/S0048577201393095 confirmed. Conference paper: 'Fatigue neurophysiology in professional and non-professional drivers', RS2002 (Road Safety Research, Policing and Education Conference), pp. 502-507, ISBN 1-876346-46-9, URL resolves (certificate name mismatch on the host, so curl needs a browser-style fetch). Jap: Expert Syst Appl 36(2, Part 1):2352-2359, 2009 confirmed via Crossref and the UTS record. De Gennaro: Clin Neurophysiol 112(10):1901-1911 confirmed.
